**Understanding the problem**
We have a tree rooted at node 0 with weighted edges and a value on each node. A *special path* is a root-to-descendant (downward) path whose node values are all distinct (a single node counts). We must return the maximum total edge length over all special paths, and among paths achieving that maximum, the minimum number of nodes.

**Example 1:** Walking down 0→1→4 gives values 2,1,3 (distinct) with length 2+4=6; 2→5 gives 2,1 with length 6. No path beats 6, and the fewest nodes on a length-6 path is 2, so the answer is `[6,2]`.

**Example 2:** Both nodes alone are special paths of length 0, so `[0,1]`.

With n up to 5·10⁴ we need roughly an O(n · something-small) traversal — a DFS over the tree where each node is processed in O(1) amortized time.
k: Every special path lies on some root-to-node vertical path, so one DFS that maintains the current root path suffices.
Along a root path, prefix distances are strictly increasing, so the best valid start for a path ending at v is the deepest forbidden ancestor plus one.
A hash map from value to its occurrence positions on the current path lets us find the last duplicate in O(1).

a.n: Approach 1: DFS with on-path occurrence stacks
a.i: Maintain the current root-to-current-node path as a stack plus each node's prefix distance. For value x, keep the stack of indices (depths) where x occurs on the current path. When entering node v, if nums[v] last occurred at depth p, any special path ending at v must start strictly below that occurrence, i.e. at depth p+1 — and since distances increase downward, starting as early as allowed maximizes length. So the candidate is dist[v] − dist[node at depth p+1] with node count depth(v) − p. Undo the push when leaving the subtree.
s: Build adjacency lists; DFS from node 0 carrying prefix distance.
On entering v, record depth; look up the previous occurrence of nums[v] on the path to get the earliest allowed start depth.
Update answer with length dist[v] − dist[startNode] and node count; prefer larger length, then fewer nodes.
Pop the occurrence and the path node when backtracking.
a.t: O(n) — each node is pushed/popped once and each hash operation is O(1) amortized.
a.sp: O(n) — adjacency lists, path stack, distance array, and the value-occurrence map.

w:
**Wrap-up**
Use the DFS-with-stacks approach — it is the natural optimal solution. Pitfalls: forgetting that a single node is a valid path (initialize the answer to `[0,1]`); forgetting to pop occurrences on backtrack; using the *first* rather than the *last* previous occurrence (only the closest duplicate constrains the path). Follow-ups: extend to "at most one duplicated value" (see 3486), or report the actual path.
